digest.top_line: Alliance A071801: fSRS beats single-fraction SRS after brain met resection, 1 year surgical bed control 87% vs 81% (p=0.046), mOS 29 vs 20 mo (HR=0.69).
digest.tldr: Fractionation and dose questions dominated: fSRS won postop for brain mets, 30 Gy was non-inferior to 40 Gy in stage I-II DLBCL in CR, while postprostatectomy HYPORT carried more G3 GU AEs (13% vs 3%). Protons gave no OS gain over photons in unresectable HCC (HR 1.30), nor did early TTFields in ndGBM (HR 0.953).

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Randomized, open-label, global phase 3**, 1:1, randomized before RT/TMZ. **N=981**, accrued Dec 2020 to Jan 2024. Stratified by MGMT promoter methylation status and extent of resection.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Adults with **ndGBM (WHO 2016 classification)**, recovered from maximal safe resection (biopsy allowed), KPS threshold 70 (inequality sign not rendered in source), RT/TMZ planned <8 weeks after surgery. Median age 60 (22-86), 65.1% male, **38.9% MGMT methylated**, 5.4% IDH mutant.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: TTFields (200 kHz) started **concurrently with RT/TMZ** (Early Start, n=492) or **with adjuvant TMZ** (Maintenance Start, n=489). TTFields recommended until second disease progression in both arms. Median device use 7.7 m vs 6.1 m.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: RT with TMZ in both arms. **Dose, fractionation, target volume and array management during RT are not reported in source.**

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** overall survival. **Secondary:** PFS, 1-, 2- and 3-year survival rate, ORR, safety. Kaplan-Meier with stratified log-rank test.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Primary **not met** in ITT (see table). PFS and ORR not different between arms, values not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Device-related AEs **76.2% Early Start vs 59.2% Maintenance Start**, mostly grade 1-2 skin-related. Grade 3+ rates and RT interruption not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: EF-14 established TTFields added to maintenance TMZ after chemoRT, which the source names as current standard and which is the control arm here. TRIDENT asks only whether starting earlier adds to that, and in ITT it **does not**.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents adults with ndGBM (WHO 2016) after maximal safe resection or biopsy who are planned for RT/TMZ and TTFields. Does not represent pts not receiving TTFields at all, since both arms used the device.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The between-arm exposure contrast is small (median use **7.7 m vs 6.1 m**) and **~25% never started maintenance**, which dilutes a timing effect. The MGMT signal conditions on device usage after randomization, with no subgroup n, interaction test or ITT MGMT-methylated result in source.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: A timing-null result, not a device-null one. The post hoc MGMT-methylated finding (**HR 0.683**, p=0.03) is a hypothesis for a prospective trial, and the abstract's "clinically meaningful" framing outruns a per-protocol-usage subset.

studies.interpretation:
The question here was narrow, and the result should be read at the same width. TRIDENT did not test whether TTFields work in ndGBM. Both arms received the device, with the control arm following the maintenance schedule that EF-14 established and that the abstract itself describes as standard. The only thing randomized was whether the arrays went on at the start of RT/TMZ or at the start of adjuvant TMZ. A flat OS comparison therefore says nothing for or against the device, and should not be recruited into either side of that older argument.

As a test of timing, the trial is large and the primary endpoint is the right one. OS is insensitive to the open-label design, which matters more for the PFS, ORR and device-attributed AE comparisons. The ITT estimate of HR 0.953 with a 95% CI of 0.82 to 1.10 excludes a large benefit from early start but leaves room for a modest one. Two features make a modest effect hard to detect. The exposure contrast the randomization actually produced was small, with median device use of 7.7 m vs 6.1 m. And ~25% of pts across both arms never started the maintenance phase, so a meaningful share of the control arm likely had little or no device exposure while the experimental arm had at least the chemoRT window. That should have favored Early Start if anything, and it still did not separate the curves.

The MGMT-methylated finding needs to be handled with care. It is conditioned twice: first on per protocol device usage during RT/TMZ, a post-randomization behavior that tracks with fitness and with not progressing early, and then on methylation status. The abstract does not state how many pts are in it, how the comparison group was defined for an arm that by design wore no device during RT, or whether an interaction test or any multiplicity control was applied. Medians of 33.8 m vs 23.8 m in both groups sit far above the ITT medians of 17.7 m and 17.5 m, which is itself evidence of how strongly the subset was selected. MGMT status was a stratification factor, so an ITT comparison within methylated tumors would be the cleaner analysis, and it is not in the source.

For a radiation oncologist the practical read is that the abstract supports feasibility but supplies none of the parameters needed to act on it. RT dose and fractionation, how arrays were managed around daily treatment, scalp dose, treatment interruptions and grade 3+ skin toxicity are all unreported. What is reported is a higher device-related AE rate, 76.2% vs 59.2%, mostly grade 1-2 skin. The WHO 2016 eligibility also admitted 5.4% IDH-mutant tumors, which current classification would not call glioblastoma. Maintenance start remains the reference schedule. Early start in MGMT-methylated disease is a hypothesis that would need its own prospective trial to be wrong or right.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Wearing TTFields through RT/TMZ raised device-related AEs to 76.2% vs 59.2% (mostly grade 1-2 skin) with no OS, PFS or ORR difference. RT dose, fractionation and array handling during RT are not reported in source, so nothing here argues for building arrays into the chemoRT course.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Sequencing stays as is: TTFields with adjuvant TMZ gave mOS 17.5 m vs 17.7 m with early start (HR 0.953, p=0.52). The MGMT-methylated signal (HR 0.683, p=0.03) comes from a post hoc per-protocol-usage subset with no n reported, so MGMT status is not yet a selector for earlier start.

open_questions: Does early TTFields improve OS in MGMT-methylated ndGBM when tested prospectively?
Scalp dose and RT interruption with arrays worn during RT/TMZ

studies.name: NRG-CC009
studies.tldr: Neurocognitive failure no different for SRS vs HA-WBRT + memantine in SCLC brain mets (adjusted HR 0.83, p=0.39); OS 17.4 vs 8.6 mo favoring SRS.
details: 📊 1° EP (time to neurocognitive failure) not met: Gray's test p=0.66

details.text: 📊 SRS vs HA-WBRT + memantine, adjusted analyses

details: 📊 No difference in adjusted intracranial failure, neurological mortality, salvage therapy, or treatment-related G3-5 AEs; effect sizes not reported in source
🔍 Phase III, 1:1 randomization, 151 pts, Feb 2021 to June 2026, stratified by DS-GPA and BM number
🔍 No upper limit on BM number after amendment (initially 10); median 2 BM (range 1-26, IQR 1-5)
🔍 Neurocognitive failure assessed by HVLT-R, COWA, and Trail Making, with death without failure as a competing risk
⚠️ Median f/u 9.5 mo for surviving pts
⚠️ OS was a secondary endpoint; the trial was powered for a 17% absolute reduction in neurocognitive failure (91 events)
⚠️ Event count, SRS dose/fractionation, HA-WBRT dose, and systemic therapy not reported in source
⚠️ Eligibility thresholds (5 mm from hippocampi, 4 cm diameter, 30 cm total volume) print without inequality symbols in the portal text
🔗 Fills the gap left by historical SRS trials, which excluded SCLC BM; the WBRT comparator is the HA-WBRT + memantine standard

verdict.rationale: Randomised phase III against the WBRT standard: neurocognitive primary not met, but OS and CNS control did not favor WBRT. OS is secondary, f/u 9.5 mo.
verdict.audience: SCLC brain mets, no cap on BM number (median 2, IQR 1-5)

studies.significance: The RT read is what SRS did not cost: adjusted intracranial failure, neurological death, and salvage therapy were no different from HA-WBRT + memantine, so omitting whole-brain coverage carried no measured CNS penalty. The neurocognitive advantage that justifies SRS in other histologies did not appear here (adjusted HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.53-1.28).
studies.monday_clinic: In SCLC with a limited number of brain mets (trial median 2, IQR 1-5), this supports SRS as an alternative to HA-WBRT + memantine; pts with many BM were eligible (range up to 26) but sparsely represented, so the read is thinner there.

primary_endpoint.name: Time to neurocognitive failure
primary_endpoint.stat_detail: 95% CI 0.53-1.28, p=0.39; Gray's test p=0.66, not met

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Phase III**, randomized **1:1**, **151 pts** assigned February 2021 to June 2026. Stratified by DS-GPA and number of BM. Median follow-up for surviving pts **9.5 months**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: SCLC brain metastases, **no upper limit on BM number** (initially 10, later amended). Median BM **2** (range 1-26, IQR 1-5). Size and volume thresholds (5 mm from the hippocampi, 4 cm largest diameter, 30 cm total volume) print without inequality symbols in the portal text.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **SRS** vs **HA-WBRT + memantine**. Dose, fractionation, and SRS platform are not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** time to neurocognitive failure (HVLT-R, COWA, Trail Making), cumulative incidence with death without failure as a competing risk. **Secondary:** OS, intracranial progression, neurological death, salvage therapies, AEs. Powered at 85% for a **17% absolute reduction** with 91 events.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **Primary not met**; OS favored SRS. Arm-level figures are in the table. CNS control endpoints and G3-5 treatment-related AEs showed no difference in adjusted analyses, with no effect sizes given.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Historical SRS vs WBRT trials excluded SCLC, which left WBRT as the default here. NRG CC001 set HA-WBRT + memantine as the neurocognitive-sparing WBRT standard, so this comparator is the strongest WBRT arm available. FIRE-SCLC supplied the retrospective case for first-line SRS that this trial tests prospectively.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents SCLC brain metastases with a limited number of lesions (median 2, IQR 1-5). Does not represent pts with extensive BM burden, who were eligible but few.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The observed event count is not reported against the **91 events** the design required. No per-arm neurocognitive failure rates, no data on systemic therapy or extracranial disease by arm, and no account of what drove the OS gap.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The trial failed its own hypothesis and still weakens the case for WBRT: without a neurocognitive or CNS-control advantage for whole-brain treatment, the argument for it rests on habit. The **OS difference is hypothesis-generating**, not a tested claim.

studies.interpretation:
The trial was built on a premise borrowed from other histologies: that SRS spares cognition relative to whole-brain treatment. That premise was established against conventional WBRT. NRG-CC009 tested it against the version of WBRT that NRG CC001 had already shown to be gentler on cognition, hippocampal avoidance with memantine, and the neurocognitive gap did not materialize (adjusted HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.53-1.28). One reading is that HA-WBRT + memantine has closed much of the distance. The other is that the trial could not see a real difference. The design assumed a 17% absolute reduction and 91 events, the abstract does not state how many events accrued among 151 pts, and the interval is wide enough to hold a clinically meaningful benefit as well as none. A null primary here is not evidence of equivalence.

The competing-risk structure matters for how to read that null. Neurocognitive failure was analysed with death without failure as a competing event, and the design assumed 29.8% of pts in both arms would die without failing. If survival differed between arms, as the OS result suggests, the arms did not carry the same exposure to cognitive testing. Longer survival gives more time to register a decline, which would work against SRS on this endpoint. The abstract gives no per-arm cumulative incidence, so this cannot be checked from the source.

The OS result (median 17.4 vs 8.6 mo, adjusted HR 0.60, p=0.016) is the number that will travel, and it deserves the most caution. It is a secondary endpoint in a 151-pt trial with 9.5 months of median follow-up in survivors. There is no obvious mechanism by which the choice of brain RT doubles nothing and yet extends survival when intracranial failure and neurological death were no different between arms. Candidate explanations sit outside the abstract: differences in time off systemic therapy, tolerance of subsequent treatment, or imbalance in extracranial disease despite balanced baseline characteristics. None is reported. Until the full paper shows cause of death and systemic therapy delivery by arm, the defensible claim is that SRS was not worse for survival.

What the trial does establish for an RT reader is narrower and more useful. In a population where most pts had few lesions (median 2, IQR 1-5), leaving the uninvolved brain untreated did not produce a measured excess of intracranial failure, salvage therapy, or neurological death in adjusted analyses. That is the prospective, randomised confirmation that FIRE-SCLC could only suggest retrospectively, and it addresses the specific fear behind WBRT in SCLC, that occult disease makes focal treatment futile.

The open edge is burden. The cap on BM number was removed, and the range reached 26, but the interquartile range shows few such pts were enrolled. Technique also gates transfer: the source gives no SRS dose or fractionation, and no detail on surveillance imaging, which is what makes an SRS-first strategy safe in a histology with a high rate of new lesions.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The RT read is what SRS did not cost: adjusted intracranial failure, neurological death, and salvage therapy were no different from HA-WBRT + memantine, so omitting whole-brain coverage carried no measured CNS penalty. The neurocognitive advantage seen in other histologies did not appear (adjusted HR 0.83, 95% CI 0.53-1.28).

open_questions: What drives the OS gap when intracranial failure and neurological death were no different?
Does SRS hold up in SCLC with high BM number?
SRS dose, fractionation, and surveillance schedule used

primary_endpoint.name: Time to surgical bed failure
primary_endpoint.stat_detail: 1 year surgical bed control, fSRS vs SRS, p=0.046

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Phase III** multi-institutional cooperative group randomized trial, **242 randomized** between October 2019 and October 2022. Stratified by age (60 years cut), targeted therapy or immunotherapy use within 4 weeks after RT, and maximal resection cavity diameter (3cm cut). Median follow-up **48 months**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **1 to 4 brain metastases** with resection of **one lesion >2cm**. Baseline characteristics reported as well-balanced; median surgical cavity target volume 16.5 for fSRS and 14.8 for SRS (p=0.41, units printed as cm in source).

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **SRS:** 12-20Gy by volume in 1 fraction. **fSRS:** 27Gy/3 for <30cc or 30Gy/5 for >30cc. Intact metastases received SRS or fSRS per assigned arm, so fractionation differed across all treated lesions, not only the cavity.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** time to surgical bed failure. **Secondary:** local control of intact brain metastases, overall survival, radiation necrosis.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Primary endpoint met in favor of fSRS, with OS and intact-lesion control moving the same direction (see table). No HR or CI for the primary endpoint in source.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **No significant differences** in adverse event rates between arms. Grade 1+ radiation necrosis **14%** fSRS vs **10%** SRS; grade 1+ cerebral edema 8% vs 9%. Symptomatic or higher-grade necrosis not broken out in source.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: N107C set postoperative single-fraction SRS as a standard against WBRT, and the MD Anderson randomised trial of cavity SRS vs observation tied local failure to larger cavities. This trial tests fractionation as the answer to that size problem, a practice the source describes as often favored but lacking high-level comparison.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pts with 1 to 4 brain metastases after resection of one lesion >2cm, treated with postoperative cavity radiosurgery. Does not represent unresected-only disease, neoadjuvant SRS candidates, or pts managed with WBRT.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Abstract only: the time-to-event primary is reported as a 1 year rate with a p-value near threshold, with no HR, CI, or per-arm N. Cavity-size subgroup results, the split between 27Gy/3 and 30Gy/5, leptomeningeal failure, and cause of death are not reported.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The local-control gain is modest and the survival difference is larger than that gain alone would predict, which points at intact-lesion control, neurologic death, or chance in a secondary endpoint. Authors conclude fSRS **should be considered a standard of care** after resection of larger brain metastasis; the necrosis data do not add a safety argument.

studies.interpretation:
The source frames this trial as the randomised comparison that fractionated cavity radiosurgery never had. Postoperative single-fraction SRS became a standard through N107C and the MD Anderson cavity trial, and the weakness that work exposed was local control as the target grew. Fractionation spread into practice on retrospective series and radiobiologic reasoning. Here the prespecified primary endpoint is positive: 1 year surgical bed control of 87% with fSRS versus 81% with SRS, p=0.046.

How much weight that carries depends on details the abstract withholds. The endpoint is time to surgical bed failure, yet the result is given as a landmark rate and a p-value sitting close to the threshold, with no hazard ratio, no confidence interval, and no per-arm denominators. A single-fraction arm controlling 81% of cavities at 1 year is not a failing comparator, so the question for the full report is whether the curves continue to diverge across the 48 months of median follow-up or whether the difference is established early and then holds flat. A reader should treat the direction as credible and the magnitude as provisional.

The survival result is the harder one to interpret. Median OS of 29 versus 20 months, HR=0.69, p=0.035, and a multivariable model that barely moves it (HR=0.68, p=0.032), is a larger effect than a modest difference in cavity control would be expected to produce. Comparisons of local brain-directed strategies have generally not shifted survival. Two features of the design offer a partial explanation. Intact metastases were treated according to the assigned arm, so the experiment is fractionation across every treated lesion, and intact-lesion failure was 11% with SRS versus 4% with fSRS (p=0.063). The other explanations are less comfortable: chance in one of several secondary endpoints, or an imbalance in systemic therapy after radiotherapy that stratification on planned use within 4 weeks would not capture. The source gives no cause of death, and without a neurologic versus systemic split the survival finding is better held as a hypothesis than as a second reason to change practice.

The toxicity data cut against a common rationale. Fractionation is often justified as kinder to surrounding brain, but grade 1+ radiation necrosis was 14% with fSRS and 10% with SRS, without a significant difference. Grade 1+ includes imaging-only change, and symptomatic rates are not reported, so this neither condemns nor supports fSRS on safety. It does mean the argument rests on control.

Transfer to practice has two gaps. Median cavity target volumes of 16.5 and 14.8 sit below the 30cc threshold, so the 27Gy/3 schedule probably carried most of the fSRS arm, and the evidence for 30Gy/5 in the largest cavities may be thin; the split is not reported. Eligibility began at a resected lesion >2cm, which reaches cavities many clinicians would still treat in one fraction, and although cavity diameter at 3cm was a stratification factor, no subgroup result is given. Leptomeningeal failure and any comparison with neoadjuvant radiosurgery sit outside what this abstract can answer.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Intact metastases were also treated per arm, so the OS signal (median 29 vs 20 months, HR=0.69, p=0.035) reflects a fractionation strategy across all treated lesions, not only the cavity. fSRS did not lower grade 1+ radiation necrosis (14% vs 10%), so the case for fractionating rests on control, not safety.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: PACE is a **phase III open-label multiple-cohort RCT**; PACE-A randomised **1:1** to SBRT or prostatectomy. **123** randomised (60 prostatectomy, 63 SBRT) between August 2012 and February 2022. Sexual outcomes analysed **by treatment received**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Early localised prostate cancer, **cT1-T2, Gleason ≤3+4, PSA ≤20 ng/mL**, and **suitable for prostatectomy**. Baseline median EPIC-26 sexual domain score was 62 in the prostatectomy group and 79 in the SBRT group.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **36.25Gy/5 fractions** delivered in 1-2 weeks. **ADT not permitted**. Platform, margins and target volume not stated in source.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Comparator was prostatectomy by open, laparoscopic or robot-assisted approach. Nerve-sparing status not stated in source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Co-primary (previously reported):** 2-year bowel and urinary symptoms. **Secondary, reported here through 5 years:** EPIC-26 sexual domain score, proportion with MCID (≥11-point reduction), IIEF-5, clinician-reported CTCAE grade ≥2 erectile dysfunction. Significance threshold **p<0.01**.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: All patient-reported measures favoured SBRT in direction; **only IIEF-5 met the prespecified p<0.01 threshold**. Clinician-graded erectile dysfunction was similar between groups.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: ProtecT randomised prostatectomy against external beam RT given with ADT, so its sexual-function comparison carried a hormonal confound that PACE-A avoids. PACE-A is described by its authors as the first randomised comparison of SBRT and prostatectomy with long-term sexual outcomes.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents men with cT1-T2, Gleason ≤3+4, PSA ≤20 ng/mL localised prostate cancer who are fit for prostatectomy and treated without ADT. Does not represent higher-risk disease, men receiving ADT with RT, or men unfit for surgery.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Baseline sexual scores were unbalanced (median **62 vs 79**), and the MCID analysis rests on **22 and 35** men. Surgical approach was mixed and nerve-sparing use is not reported. Accrual ran from 2012 to 2022, so technique on both sides spans a decade.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The direction is consistent across three patient-reported measures, which carries more weight than any single p-value here. SBRT still produced a decline (median change **-17**), so the result is a relative advantage, not preserved function. Cancer control is not reported in this abstract.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this report is randomisation. Sexual function after surgery versus radiotherapy for localised prostate cancer has mostly been compared in observational cohorts, where the men who choose surgery differ at baseline from those who choose radiation, and in ProtecT, where the radiotherapy arm received ADT and so carried a hormonal confound on exactly this endpoint. PACE-A removes that confound by design. ADT was not permitted, so whatever happened to erectile function in the radiation arm reflects 36.25Gy in 5 fractions and nothing else.

The direction of the result is what most readers would predict. The confidence it deserves is lower than the abstract's language suggests. The authors set p<0.01 as their threshold for statistical significance and then describe sexual function as significantly worse after prostatectomy on the strength of an EPIC-26 change with p = 0.02 and an MCID comparison with p=0.03. By the trial's own rule only the IIEF-5 difference (p<0.001) qualifies. The clinician-graded endpoint did not separate at all (p=0.48). That discordance is familiar: CTCAE erectile dysfunction grading is a blunt instrument next to a validated questionnaire. It still means one of four measures is formally positive.

The analysis was by treatment received, not by allocation. In a trial asking men to accept a coin flip between an operation and five outpatient fractions, departures from allocation are not random. In the prostatectomy arm 50 men had the operation, 3 had chemoradiotherapy and 6 withdrew; in the SBRT arm 60 were treated as allocated. An as-treated comparison in that setting loses part of the protection randomisation was supposed to provide. Baseline medians of 62 and 79 show the analysed groups already differed on the outcome itself. Change from baseline partly addresses that, and a lower starting score leaves less room to fall, which if anything works against the surgical arm showing the larger decline. Participant-reported data at 5 years came from 30/50 and 38/60, and the MCID analysis from 22 and 35 men. Whether the non-responders were the men doing well or badly is unknown, and it could differ by arm.

Transferability has its own gaps. Accrual ran from August 2012 to February 2022, a long window for 123 men, which points to a selected population. Prostatectomy could be open, laparoscopic or robot assisted, and the abstract is silent on nerve sparing. On the radiation side, platform, margins and any vessel- or bulb-sparing constraints are not given. A median EPIC-26 of 58 after SBRT is still a fall from 79. Radiation-related erectile decline is typically gradual while surgical decline is immediate with partial recovery, so the gap at 5 years is one cross-section of two different curves.

What this changes is the counselling conversation for a surgical candidate with low or favourable intermediate risk disease for whom erectile function is a deciding factor: there are now randomised patient-reported data, free of ADT, that favour SBRT. It leaves cancer control untouched, since none is reported here, and it has to be read alongside the bowel and urinary co-primaries reported earlier. It would be wrong mainly if missing responders differed systematically between arms.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: No ADT was permitted, so the SBRT trajectory (median EPIC-26 79 to 58) is attributable to 36.25Gy/5 fractions alone. By the trial's own p<0.01 rule only IIEF-5 (median 19 vs 5) is positive, and clinician-graded ED was similar (27% vs 35%). Counselling data, not a claim of preserved function.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Median EPIC-26 sexual score fell from 62 to 17 after prostatectomy, with 18/22 (82%) crossing the MCID. Approach was mixed (open, laparoscopic, robot assisted) and nerve-sparing use is not reported, so the figure may not reflect a contemporary nerve-sparing robotic series. Analysis was by treatment received.

open_questions: Does the sexual-function gap hold against nerve-sparing robotic prostatectomy alone?
Does SBRT erectile function keep declining beyond 5 years?
Oncologic outcomes for SBRT vs prostatectomy in PACE-A

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Secondary analysis** of NRG/RTOG 9601, a phase 3 trial of sRT ± high-dose bicalutamide, using GC scores (Veracyte) from a prior translational project. **GC-available cohort n=352**, median follow-up **18.2 years**. Multivariable Cox or Fine-Gray models, adjusted (s)HR with 95% CI.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Pts treated with sRT on NRG/RTOG 9601 who had a GC score. Median GC **0.59** (Q1-Q3 0.42-0.76); 29%, 23%, 38% and 11% were low, intermediate, high and very high risk. Other baseline features not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: sRT with or without **high-dose bicalutamide** (AAT). Bicalutamide dose and duration not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Salvage RT in both arms. Dose, fractionation and target volume **not reported in source**.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary objective:** prognostic impact of GC (per 0.1) on PCSM. **Secondary:** OS, MFS, DM. Additional: PCSM and OS by pre-defined GC strata, and PCSM benefit of AAT by GC (<0.6 vs ≥0.6) within pre-sRT PSA subgroup (<0.7 vs ≥0.7).

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: GC was **independently prognostic for every profiled endpoint** (tables above). The AAT-by-GC estimates are absolute 15-year PCSM differences with **no significant interaction** in either PSA stratum.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Extends the earlier GC validation in this same trial with final outcomes, and layers GC onto the prior 9601 finding that pre-sRT PSA predicts AAT benefit. GETUG-AFU 16, NRG/RTOG 0534 (SPPORT) and RADICALS-HD tested ADT with post-prostatectomy RT; none is addressed in this source.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents pts given sRT ± high-dose bicalutamide on NRG/RTOG 9601 with a GC score available (n=352). Does not represent pts receiving contemporary ADT with sRT, which this analysis did not test.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: AAT benefit by GC is given as point estimates only: **no CIs, no cell sizes**. PCSM was chosen as primary for this secondary analysis because of suspected other-cause mortality with bicalutamide, which sets aside the endpoint where AAT harm would show. Whether the GC-available subset matches the full trial is not reported.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The prognostic claim is well supported at long follow-up. The predictive claim is not: the GC gradient runs in opposite directions in the two PSA strata. The authors frame GC-guided selection for modern ADT in early sRT as a **hypothesis**, which is the right ceiling.

studies.interpretation:
Two claims sit in this abstract and they deserve different levels of confidence. The first is prognostic: GC score, modelled continuously per 0.1 and adjusted for clinical covariates, tracks with PCSM, OS, MFS and DM at a median follow-up of 18.2 years. This is an update of a validation already performed in the same trial, now with final outcomes, and the direction and consistency across four endpoints make it hard to argue with. The 15-year contrast between the extremes is stark, PCSM 4% vs 52% and OS 75% vs 25%, though it compares the 29% of the cohort with low scores against the 11% with very high scores. The abstract does not report the two middle strata, which is where most counseling decisions actually fall.

The second claim is predictive: that GC might identify who needs hormone therapy with sRT. Here the data are much thinner. At pre-sRT PSA <0.7, the 15-year PCSM benefit from AAT was -2% with GC <0.6 and 16% with GC ≥0.6, which reads as a clean selection story. At PSA ≥0.7 the same split gives 12% and 6%, with the larger benefit in the lower GC group. If GC were a general predictor of hormone benefit, one would expect the gradient to point the same way in both strata. It does not. The authors attribute the non-significant interaction tests to limited power, and that is plausible, but the reversal is equally compatible with noise from carving 352 pts into four cells. No confidence intervals or cell sizes are given, so the reader cannot judge how far any one of these estimates could move.

The endpoint choice also matters. PCSM was selected as the primary endpoint of this secondary analysis because high-dose bicalutamide may raise other-cause mortality, an effect the authors suggest may not occur with contemporary ADT. That reasoning is defensible, yet it removes from view the endpoint on which the hormone arm could look worse. An OS version of the same four-cell table would be the natural companion and is not in the source.

Transferability is the last gap. The hormone agent tested was high-dose bicalutamide, and the conclusion reaches toward modern ADT in early sRT. Trials such as GETUG-AFU 16, NRG/RTOG 0534 (SPPORT) and RADICALS-HD studied ADT with post-prostatectomy RT, and the question of whether GC modifies benefit in those settings is not answered here. RT dose, fractionation and target volume are also absent from the abstract, so the radiotherapy backdrop against which hormone benefit was measured cannot be compared to current practice from this source alone.

The practical read: GC is a credible long-term risk ranker for pts headed to sRT, and that alone can inform how a clinician frames prognosis. The suggestion that a low GC score at low PSA marks pts who gain nothing from hormones is a single unreplicated cell with a negative point estimate and no interval. It would be wrong if the GC-available subset differs systematically from the full trial, or if the low-PSA pattern fails to appear in a cohort treated with contemporary ADT. A prospective GC-stratified comparison is what would settle it.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The sRT decision in play is hormone omission at low pre-sRT PSA: at PSA <0.7, 15y PCSM benefit from AAT was -2% with GC <0.6 vs 16% with GC ≥0.6. At PSA ≥0.7 the gradient reverses (12% vs 6%), so GC ranks risk more reliably than it selects for hormones. RT dose and volume not reported.

open_questions: Does GC predict benefit from contemporary ADT with early sRT?
Do intermediate and high GC strata separate on 15-year PCSM and OS?
Does the AAT-by-GC pattern hold for OS, not just PCSM?

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Phase 3** trial, **296 men randomized** (152 COPORT, 144 HYPORT). This is the 5-year report; **median follow-up 7 years** (range: 0 to 8). Blinding, stratification and site count are not stated in source.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Postprostatectomy men with either a **detectable post-op PSA** (source prints "=0.1 ng/mL") and **pT2/3 pNX/0** disease, or an **undetectable PSA (<0.1 ng/mL)** with pT3 disease or pT2 with a positive surgical margin. The split between these two groups is not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **HYPORT: 62.5 Gy to the prostate bed in 25 fractions of 2.5 Gy.** **COPORT: 66.6 Gy in 37 fractions of 1.8 Gy**, 48% more fractions. Pelvic nodal RT, technique and ADT use are not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary (reported at 2 years):** patient-reported GU and GI toxicity by EPIC, where HYPORT was noninferior. **Secondary, reported here:** EQ-5D quality of life, AEs, overall survival, prostate-cancer specific survival, and biochemical failure (PSA 0.4 ng/mL and rising; source prints the operator as "=").

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Arm-level figures are in the table. **No difference** in 5-yr EPIC bowel or urinary change scores, EQ-5D change, or 5-yr BF; 31 deaths, 4 (13%) due to prostate cancer.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **Grade 3 AEs 16% (23 men) HYPORT vs 7% (11 men) COPORT, p=0.02**, driven by **grade 3 renal and urinary disorders, 13% vs 3% (p=0.003)**: noninfective cystitis 7% vs 0%, hematuria 6% vs 0.7%. No grade 4-5 RT-related AEs, one grade 3 stricture (COPORT), and time to grade 3 AEs did not differ (p=0.4).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Moderate hypofractionation for the intact prostate rests on large randomized trials such as CHHiP and PROFIT; the postoperative bed has lacked comparable randomized data. The authors state the grade 3 GU rates, including the excess with HYPORT, were **consistent with contemporary series**, which the source does not name.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents men after prostatectomy with pT2/3 pNX/0 disease and a detectable PSA, or an undetectable PSA with pT3 or margin-positive pT2, treated to the prostate bed. Does not represent pelvic nodal RT or any setting outside these eligibility groups, and ADT use is not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The patient-reported reassurance rests on **56% EPIC and 51% EQ-5D compliance at 5 years**, with no account of who dropped out. **BF is a secondary endpoint with no stated noninferiority margin**, and p-values for the cystitis and hematuria differences are not given.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: HYPORT buys a shorter course at the cost of a **physician-reported grade 3 cystitis/hematuria excess** that patient-reported scores do not register. Biochemical control looks comparable (5-yr BF 21% vs 18%, p=0.3) but the trial was built around toxicity, so equivalence of disease control is suggested, not established.

studies.interpretation:
Moderate hypofractionation became standard for the intact prostate on the strength of large randomized trials such as CHHiP and PROFIT, but the postoperative bed is a different target. The bladder neck and the vesicourethral anastomosis sit inside the high-dose volume, and the randomized evidence for larger fractions there has been thin. GU003 is the randomized test of that extrapolation, and one design choice governs how to read it: the trial was built around patient-reported GU and GI toxicity, with HYPORT already shown noninferior at 2 years, and not around disease control.

The 5-year update splits according to who is doing the reporting. Physician-graded grade 3 renal and urinary events were 13% with HYPORT against 3% with COPORT (p=0.003), driven by noninfective cystitis and hematuria, while EPIC urinary change scores (-8.0 vs -5.7, p=0.4) did not separate. Both can be true at once. A bleeding episode that prompts intervention is graded 3 by the clinician without necessarily moving a urinary domain score measured years later. But the patient-reported side rests on 56% EPIC compliance at 5 years, and the abstract does not say whether men who had an event were as likely to return a questionnaire as men who did not. The reassurance from the PROs is softer than the p-values alone suggest.

The pattern of events is informative for an RT reader. Time to grade 3 AEs did not differ between arms (p=0.4), which reads as more events with HYPORT, not earlier ones. There were no grade 4-5 RT-related events, and the single grade 3 stricture occurred on the COPORT arm, so the specific fear that 2.5 Gy fractions would injure the anastomosis is not borne out here. What the larger fraction size appears to cost is bladder mucosal bleeding.

On disease control, a 5-year BF of 21% vs 18% (p=0.3) is a secondary endpoint in 296 men with no noninferiority margin stated in the source. A nonsignificant p-value is not evidence of equivalence, and with 31 deaths, 4 from prostate cancer, survival endpoints cannot discriminate between arms. The comparison is also against 66.6 Gy, so comparable control is relative to that dose and not to an escalated salvage regimen. Eligibility mixed adjuvant-type pts (undetectable PSA with adverse pathology) and salvage-type pts (detectable PSA). Since RADICALS-RT and RAVES moved practice toward early salvage, the detectable-PSA stratum is the one closest to current referrals, and the abstract does not report outcomes by that split.

What this changes is narrow and concrete: prostate-bed-only RT can be offered in 25 fractions, where COPORT's 37 fractions are 48% more, with a quantified grade 3 cystitis and hematuria risk to disclose. It leaves untouched whether the same holds with pelvic nodal fields or concurrent ADT, neither of which the source reports. The read would be wrong if PRO dropout was informative, or if bladder events keep accruing beyond the 7-year median follow-up.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: 62.5 Gy/25 fx to the prostate bed carries more physician-graded grade 3 cystitis (7% vs 0%) and hematuria (6% vs 0.7%) than 66.6 Gy/37 fx, while 5-yr EPIC urinary change (-8.0 vs -5.7, p=0.4) and 5-yr BF (21% vs 18%, p=0.3) do not separate. This informs the prostate-bed fractionation choice, with bleeding risk part of consent.

open_questions: Does prostate-bed hypofractionation hold with pelvic nodal RT or concurrent ADT?
Ultrahypofractionated (SBRT) prostate-bed RT vs moderate hypofractionation
Do grade 3 cystitis/hematuria events keep accruing beyond 7-yr follow-up?

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Prospective, **randomized phase II**, 1:1 allocation after neoadjuvant chemo. **102 pts** targeted and enrolled, anticipating a 15% drop out before surgery; 4 withdrew after enrollment. Median follow-up among all enrolled pts **3.4 [2.6, 5.1] years**.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **Resectable, borderline, or locally advanced (LA) type A PDAC**, ECOG 0-2, **> 1 month of neoadjuvant chemo**. Median age 65 (34-82); 38%/42%/20% resectable, borderline, and LA type A. Prior chemo was FOLFIRINOX (79%), gemcitabine/nab-paclitaxel (12%), or other (9%), with 92% receiving more than 2 months.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **Chemo-RT:** 50.4 Gy/28 fractions with weekly gemcitabine or capecitabine. **SBRT:** 25 Gy/5 to elective nodes and 33-40 Gy in 5 to the primary, **without concurrent chemo**. Most SBRT pts were treated using 1.5 T adaptive MRI guidance.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** pathologic node positivity, hypothesizing lower rates with chemo-RT. **Secondary:** PFS, OS, patient-reported QOL (PROMIS), physician-reported toxicity, surgical complications, translational endpoints.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Arm-level figures are in the table. **83/98 (84.7%)** completed all intended therapy including surgical resection, equal in both arms.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: **No difference in surgical complications**; no rates given. Physician-reported toxicity was a secondary endpoint but is not reported in the abstract. PROMIS physical function, global physical health, and fatigue were **better preserved with SBRT** (p = < 0.05).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Alliance A021501 tested preop SBRT or hypofractionated RT against chemotherapy alone, and PREOPANC established gemcitabine-based preop chemo-RT against upfront surgery. Neither compared one RT schedule with another. The authors describe this as the **first randomized trial comparing SBRT with chemo-RT** in the neoadjuvant setting for PDAC.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents resectable, borderline, or LA type A PDAC, ECOG 0-2, after > 1 month of neoadjuvant chemo and planned for preop RT then resection. Does not represent pts with no neoadjuvant chemo or those not headed to surgical resection.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Abstract only: **no per-arm allocation counts**, no QOL magnitudes or timepoints, and no figures for pathologic response or margin negativity despite the conclusion citing them. QOL is patient-reported in an unblinded comparison. Concurrent agent varied in the chemo-RT arm and primary SBRT dose ranged 33-40 Gy.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The trial shows SBRT is deliverable preop with **equal resection completion and better QOL**, and it does not show nodal sterilization differs. It does **not settle survival equivalence**: median OS 26.04 vs 42.96 mo and LRR 6 vs 2 point the same direction in a sample too small to resolve them.

studies.interpretation:
The trial was built as a superiority test in the opposite direction to how it is being read. The hypothesis was that conventionally fractionated chemo-RT, with a longer course and a concurrent radiosensitizer, would sterilize nodes better than SBRT, and pathologic node positivity was the endpoint chosen to show it. It did not: 41% with SBRT vs 38% with chemo-RT, p = 0.754. A failed superiority test in 102 pts is not a demonstration of equivalence, and the conclusion that the data support SBRT rests on the absence of a detected difference, not on a prespecified non-inferiority margin. That distinction is the whole interpretive problem.

The secondary endpoints deserve a slower read than the abstract gives them. Median OS was 26.04 mo with SBRT and 42.96 mo with chemo-RT, 3-year survival 42.6% vs 57.5%, PFS 14.28 vs 21.6 mo, and local/regional recurrence 6 vs 2 events. None reaches statistical significance, and the OS intervals (17.9 to 59.28 vs 18.72 to 54.72) overlap almost entirely, so no single comparison carries weight. But every one leans the same way, toward chemo-RT, in a trial too small to exclude a clinically meaningful gap. "No difference" is a fair statistical summary and a weak clinical one. The honest position is that the trial cannot separate a modest chemo-RT advantage from noise.

Prior randomized evidence does not help resolve it. Alliance A021501 put preop SBRT or hypofractionated RT up against chemotherapy alone, and PREOPANC tested gemcitabine-based conventional chemo-RT against upfront surgery. Each asked whether preop RT belongs in the sequence; neither asked which schedule. This trial is the first to ask that, and it does so in a contemporary population, most of whom had received FOLFIRINOX for more than 2 months before enrollment. Whether RT of any kind adds to that backbone is a question the design cannot touch, since both arms were irradiated.

Technique gates transfer. The SBRT arm was a specific package: 25 Gy/5 to elective nodes, 33-40 Gy in 5 to the primary, and mostly 1.5 T adaptive MR guidance. A center delivering CT-guided SBRT to gross disease alone is not reproducing the tested arm, and whatever nodal parity exists here may depend on the elective volume. The 6 vs 2 local/regional split is too few events to interpret, yet it is the number an RT reader should carry forward, because it is where a real dose or volume deficit would show first. The chemo-RT arm was also not uniform, with either gemcitabine or capecitabine concurrent.

The positive finding is QOL: physical function, global physical health and fatigue were better preserved with SBRT. That is plausible for a five-fraction course without concurrent chemo, but it is patient-reported in an unblinded trial and the abstract gives no magnitudes or timepoints. What changes is narrow. Where preop RT is already planned, the tolerability argument for SBRT now has randomized support and no penalty in resection completion or surgical complications. What stays open is survival, and the reading would be wrong if a larger trial showed the OS lean to be real.

The fractionation choice moves toward SBRT on QOL only where that nodal volume and platform are reproduced.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: 83/98 (84.7%) reached resection, 41 SBRT and 42 chemo-RT, with no difference in surgical complications, so the 5-fraction course did not cost operability. primary_endpoint.name: Acute toxicity T-score ratio (weekly/Q3)
primary_endpoint.stat_detail: 90% upper confidence bound 1.33, p=0.77 · phase III criteria not met

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Randomized phase II/III; this is the **phase II acute toxicity** report for the **p16-negative cohort**. **234 randomized** (118 Q3, 116 Q1) between Oct 2021 and Sept 2025; 91% completed all follow-up up to 6 months. QA modality reviews were done on a random sample of cases.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: **p16-negative locoregionally advanced SCCHN.** Median age 60; 76% male; 58% Zubrod 0; 87% former or current smokers, 70% >10 pack-years. **57% larynx**, 28% oropharynx, 15% hypopharynx; 83% T1-3 and 74% node-positive.

analysis_sections.label: Regimen
analysis_sections.body: Cisplatin **100 mg/m2 Q3 weeks** (Q3) vs cisplatin **40 mg/m2 weekly** (Q1), each with RT. Chemotherapy delivery scored per protocol or acceptable variation in 80% on Q3 vs 98% on Q1. Cumulative cisplatin dose delivered is not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **70 Gy in both arms**; fractionation, technique and target volumes are not reported in source. RT reviews were completed for 91% of sampled pts, scored per protocol or acceptable variation in **81% on Q3 vs 94% on Q1**.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** acute toxicity by T-score, the number of all treatment-related grade 3-4 AEs during treatment or within six months. To proceed to phase III, the mean T-score ratio (Q1/Q3) had to be below 1 at 1-sided p<0.1, together with a 6-month locoregional failure difference criterion (printed as '= 8%' absolute in the portal text).

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: The cohort **did not meet criteria for continuing to phase III**; arm-level values are in the tables.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Total G3-4 burden was similar, but the profile differed by schedule. **Q3** carried more G3-4 nausea (12% vs 4%), dehydration (9% vs 1%) and **acute kidney injury (11% vs 3%)**; **weekly** carried more WBC decrease (28% vs 14%) and hypomagnesemia (8% vs 2%). Late toxicity is not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The Tata Memorial randomized trial (Noronha et al.) favored Q3 over a lower weekly dose for locoregional control in a mostly postoperative population, while JCOG1008 supported weekly dosing after surgery. This cohort tests the schedule question with 70 Gy RT in p16-negative disease and gives **no toxicity support for weekly**; the source draws no comparison to either trial.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents p16-negative locoregionally advanced SCCHN, larynx-dominant with heavy smoking history, treated with 70 Gy RT and concurrent cisplatin. Does not represent the p16-positive cohort (241 pts, reported separately) or settings other than 70 Gy RT with concurrent cisplatin.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The T-score weighs every G3-4 event equally, so marrow and renal events are interchangeable in the primary. QA was scored on a **random sample**, not all cases, and per-arm cumulative cisplatin dose is missing. The portal text has lost the inequality in the LRF criterion, so the abstract alone does not show whether that half of the rule passed.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: The tolerability premise for weekly cisplatin did not hold here: toxicity was **redistributed, not reduced**. The LRF difference favors Q3 but rests on a 6-month read in a toxicity-driven phase II, so it is a direction, not an efficacy result. Pooled results for all 475 pts were deferred to the presentation.

studies.interpretation:
Weekly cisplatin spread through head and neck practice on one assumption: that it buys tolerability at little cost in disease control. This phase II was built to test the first half of that assumption with a count of high-grade events, and the first half failed. The ratio did not merely miss its threshold, it pointed the other way (1.11, with a 90% upper bound of 1.33). What the arm-level rates describe is a trade, not a saving. High-dose Q3 dosing costs nausea, dehydration and acute kidney injury, weekly dosing costs white cell count and magnesium.

That trade is where the T-score stops being informative. It treats every grade 3-4 event as one unit, so a transient WBC decrease and an episode of acute kidney injury carry identical weight. A reader who regards renal injury as the more consequential event in a pt who may need salvage systemic therapy later will read the same data as mildly favoring weekly on safety, and a reader worried about marrow suppression interrupting RT will read it the other way. The trial answers whether weekly lowers the event count. It does not answer which schedule is easier on the pt, and the abstract reports no late toxicity to help.

The locoregional failure figures deserve more caution than their confidence interval invites. Six months mostly captures persistent disease and very early progression, the phase II was sized around toxicity, and event counts are not given. The portal text has also lost the inequality sign in the go criterion, so the abstract cannot show whether the control half of the rule was satisfied on its own. Still, the direction is worth noting because of what sits beside it: the Q3 arm had the lower per protocol rates for both RT (81% vs 94%) and chemotherapy (80% vs 98%) on sampled review. A quality imbalance of that kind would be expected to work against Q3, and Q3 still had less failure. The plausible reading of the chemotherapy deviations is dose modification after toxicity, but that is inference, and the missing variable is the cumulative cisplatin dose each arm received.

Against prior randomized data, this fits the older concern more than it overturns anything. The Tata Memorial trial favored Q3 for locoregional control against a lower weekly dose in a largely postoperative population, and JCOG1008 found weekly dosing acceptable after surgery. Neither addressed intact p16-negative disease treated to full dose, which is the population here, and the larynx-dominant, heavy-smoking case mix is the one where locoregional failure drives outcome.

What changes is the justification, not necessarily the prescription. Selecting weekly because it is assumed gentler overall is no longer supported in this population. Selecting it for a specific pt with limited renal reserve remains coherent with the AE pattern. The read would weaken if longer follow-up closes the failure gap, if delivered cisplatin dose turns out similar between arms, or if the pooled analysis of all 475 pts shows a different toxicity pattern. The p16-positive cohort was reported separately and its result is not in this source.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: 6-mo LRF was 4.6% (Q3) vs 9.6% (weekly), absolute difference 5.0% (95% CI 1.0, 8.9), despite worse RT QA on Q3 (81% vs 94% per protocol or acceptable). RT quality does not explain the gap. With 70 Gy fixed, the concurrent schedule is the variable to weigh for locoregional control.
significance_by_specialty.medonc: Weekly 40 mg/m2 traded toxicities instead of lowering them: G3-4 AKI 11% vs 3% and nausea 12% vs 4% on Q3, WBC decrease 28% vs 14% and hypomagnesemia 8% vs 2% on weekly. Chemotherapy delivery was per protocol or acceptable in 80% on Q3 vs 98% on weekly; cumulative dose not reported.

primary_endpoint.stat_detail: HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.59-1.28; one-sided P = 0.0013 for non-inferiority

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Multicenter, open-label, non-inferiority phase 3**, randomized **1:1**. **432** pts enrolled April 14, 2010 to July 1, 2019; median follow-up **7.2 years**. Non-inferiority margin not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Newly diagnosed **stage I-II DLBCL** achieving **CR/CRu** after anthracycline-based chemo **with/without rituximab**. Age criterion printed as '=15 years' in the portal text. Bulk, IPI and PET status at response not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **30 Gy vs 40 Gy** consolidative **involved-site/field RT**. Fraction size, technique and the split between involved-site and involved-field volumes are not reported in source.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: **Primary:** 5-year PFS, tested for non-inferiority of 30 Gy. Also reported: OS, locoregional recurrence, acute and late toxicity including second malignancies.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Primary endpoint met (table). OS and locoregional recurrence showed **no difference between arms**; the source gives no rates or HRs for either.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Acute and late toxicities, **including second malignancies**, were comparable between arms. No rates or grades reported in source, so **no measured toxicity advantage for 30 Gy**.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The source states no prior randomized trial compared these two doses in DLBCL specifically. The UK NHL dose-reduction RCT (Lowry et al.) asked a similar de-escalation question in aggressive NHL more broadly, and ILROG guidance already favors the lower consolidative dose after CR, so this result is concordant with that direction.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents stage I-II DLBCL in CR/CRu after anthracycline-based chemo with or without rituximab, receiving consolidative involved-site/field RT. Does not represent pts with partial response or residual disease, advanced-stage DLBCL, or the question of omitting RT altogether.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Enrollment spans 2010 to 2019 with **rituximab optional** and response graded as CR/CRu, so systemic therapy and response assessment may not match current PET-adapted practice. Mixed involved-site/field volumes are not broken out. Abstract only: no event counts, no margin.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: With PFS near 90% in both arms and locoregional recurrence no different, the higher dose bought no measurable disease control in pts already in CR. What the trial does not settle is whether the lower dose reduces late effects (not shown at 7.2 years) and whether any RT is needed after a PET-negative response.

studies.interpretation:
The question here is narrow and well posed: once a pt with stage I-II DLBCL is in complete remission after anthracycline-based chemotherapy, does the consolidative dose need to be 40 Gy, or does 30 Gy do the same job. The trial answers it with a randomized comparison, a prespecified non-inferiority primary, and a median follow-up of 7.2 years, long enough that most DLBCL relapses would have declared themselves. The 5-year PFS point estimate actually sits on the side of the lower dose (90.5% vs 87.2%), and the HR of 0.87 has an upper confidence bound of 1.28. That bound is the number to hold onto, since the abstract does not print the non-inferiority margin. A reader cannot check how generous the margin was, only that the one-sided P of 0.0013 cleared it.

The direction is unsurprising. The UK randomized dose-reduction trial in NHL (Lowry et al.) already pointed toward lower doses being adequate in aggressive histologies, and ILROG guidance has favored the lower consolidative dose after CR for years. What this trial adds is a DLBCL-specific, CR-restricted randomized dataset, which the authors say did not previously exist. In centers that already use the lower dose it reads as confirmation with better evidence behind it; in centers still prescribing 40 Gy or above (the abstract cites doses from 30 to 55 Gy in use) it is the reason to stop.

Several design features should temper how far the result is stretched. Enrollment ran from 2010 to 2019 and rituximab was optional, so some fraction of the cohort received systemic therapy weaker than current standard. If anything that makes the finding more reassuring, since RT was carrying more of the load in those pts and the lower dose still held. Response is described as CR/CRu, a category from CT-era criteria, and the abstract does not say whether PET defined remission. A CT-defined CRu may include pts who would be PET-positive today, and the trial says nothing about what dose residual metabolically active disease needs. The target is given as involved-site/field, which implies a shift in volume definition during accrual; outcomes by volume are not reported.

The weakest part of the abstract is the toxicity claim. The stated rationale for de-escalation is less long-term harm, yet acute and late toxicities and second malignancies were comparable between arms. At 7.2 years that is too early for radiation-induced solid tumors or cardiac events to separate, so the benefit of the lower dose rests on dosimetric logic and not on trial data. Open-label design matters little for PFS in this setting, but no rates are given for OS, locoregional recurrence or any toxicity, so the secondary claims cannot be weighed.

The decision this moves is dose, not indication. It does not test RT omission after a PET-negative response, which is the live controversy in limited-stage DLBCL, and it does not inform doses below 30 Gy.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The local-regional read backs the PFS headline: locoregional recurrence did not differ between 30 Gy and 40 Gy involved-site/field RT, though no rates are given in the source text. Toxicity, including second malignancies, was also comparable at 7.2 years median f/u, so the late-effect gain from de-escalation is inferred, not shown.

open_questions: Can consolidative RT be omitted after PET-negative CR in limited-stage DLBCL?

studies.interpretation:
The question here is the one PROSPECT asked in a lower-risk population, moved into the immunotherapy era: if systemic therapy is active enough, can pelvic RT be left out of neoadjuvant treatment for rectal cancer. It also follows directly from TORCH, which varied where SCRT sat relative to CAPOX and toripalimab but never removed it. The premise in the abstract is functional, that RT plus surgery costs more than either alone, so the bar the no-RT arm has to clear is not equivalence on response but a functional gain large enough to justify whatever response it gives up.

On response, it gives up a lot. Overall CR was 61.5% with SCRT and 37.1% without. The decomposition is more informative than the headline. Among resected pts, pCR was 44.2% vs 32.8%, a real but moderate gap. The larger separation is in clinical responders who went to W&W, 25 vs 7. That matters in two directions. It means the resected-only pCR comparison is biased against the SCRT arm, because its best responders were removed from the surgical denominator before pathology could count them. It also means the trial's advantage for RT rests disproportionately on cCR, the component that is assessor-dependent, unblinded by necessity, and subject to later regrowth.

Several design features should temper confidence in the size of the gap. The analysis is restricted to 148 pts who completed treatment out of 192 enrolled, so it is neither intention-to-treat nor final, and the abstract offers no p-value or interval. The assessment timepoint is not given; an arm that begins with a week of RT before six cycles of systemic therapy may be assessed later from the start of treatment, and elapsed time alone raises response rates in rectal cancer. Four non-cCR pts in the no-RT arm have no resolved outcome. None of these plausibly erases the difference, but each could move it.

The finding the authors foreground, an encouraging CR rate with CAPOX plus a PD-1 inhibitor alone in pMMR disease, is the least secure claim in the abstract. Without a chemotherapy-alone arm there is no way to assign that response to toripalimab rather than to six cycles of CAPOX, and pMMR tumors are the setting where checkpoint inhibition has been least rewarding without a priming stimulus. If anything, the arm comparison reads as indirect support for RT as that stimulus, though the trial cannot separate immune priming from the direct cytoreductive effect of 25Gy/5Fx.

For the functional argument, the early disposition data cut against RT omission. In a cohort where 96.6% had at least one high-risk feature, 58 of 70 pts without RT went to surgery vs 52 of 78 with it, and the no-RT arm retained adjuvant chemoradiotherapy for positive circumferential margins at an unreported rate. Avoiding radiation proctopathy in exchange for more resections is not obviously a functional win, and anorectal function has not been reported. What would overturn the current read is a high regrowth rate among the 25 W&W pts in the SCRT arm, or a functional readout favoring the no-RT arm despite more surgery. RAPIDO is the standing reminder that early response advantages with SCRT-based TNT do not guarantee locoregional control on longer follow-up, and that is the readout to wait for.

studies.interpretation:
The question here is narrower than the headline suggests. TNT is already standard in pMMR LARC, and earlier phase II work had suggested that immunotherapy layered onto it raises complete response. What was missing was a controlled comparison at scale, and this trial supplies one: the same short-course RT, the same CAPOX, with sintilimab as the only randomized variable. That design isolates the drug cleanly. It does not test the radiotherapy, so the result should not be read as an endorsement of short-course over long-course chemoradiation as the partner for a checkpoint inhibitor. Trials such as UNION and TORCH explored short-course RT with checkpoint blockade, but neither held everything else constant against an immunotherapy-free TNT arm, which is the gap this one fills.

Confidence in the direction of the effect should be high. Overall CR was 51.9% vs 26.8% on denominators of 289 and 291, which is close to the whole randomized population, so the comparison is not built on a selected subset. The pCR figures need more care. They are computed among operated pts only, 211 in the iTNT arm and 247 in the TNT arm. Fewer iTNT pts reaching surgery is what one would expect if more of them were diverted to watch-and-wait after a clinical complete response, although the source does not give the per-arm split. Removing the best responders from the surgical denominator would, if anything, pull the iTNT pCR rate down, so the pCR gap is unlikely to be flattered by that selection. The softer component is the clinical one. A cCR is an assessor-dependent call, the source does not say whether assessment was blinded, and a clinician who knows a pt received immunotherapy may be more willing to defer surgery. That is where a skeptic should push.

The population is high risk: T3-4 in 94.9%, node-positive in 92.9%, MRF+ in 48.8%, EMVI in 45.4%, and lower tumors in 71.3%. This is the group in which sphincter loss is most at stake and organ preservation is hardest to achieve, so the result applies directly to the low rectal tumor facing a permanent stoma. It says less about the early, low-risk tumors that some organ-preservation programs select.

The cost is measurable. Grade 3-4 toxicity was 27.7% vs 19.9%, with grade 3-5 immune-related events in 3.4%. Treatment delivery did not suffer: every pt completed SCRT and chemotherapy completion was 92.9% vs 94.1%. Surgical morbidity and late effects are not reported, and the grade 3-5 category leaves open whether any immune-related event was fatal.

What the trial has not shown is the endpoint it was powered for in its phase 3 portion, 3-year DFS. Complete response is a response endpoint, and the experience with short-course TNT in RAPIDO is a reminder that early response gains do not guarantee durable locoregional control. The result would be undermined if regrowths in the watch-and-wait cohort erode the clinical component of the CR advantage, or if DFS curves fail to separate in a pMMR population where checkpoint blockade has historically done little on its own. Until those data arrive, this supports discussing the regimen as an organ-preservation option, not treating it as a new standard.

analysis_sections.body: Represents MM pts with an uncomplicated painful bone lesion, mostly ECOG 0-1 (89%) with a median of 1 prior line. Does not represent complicated bone lesions or bone metastases from solid tumors.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Missing assessments grow from **2/70 at 4 weeks to 25/70 at 6 months**, and reasons are not given, so the late per-protocol rates are vulnerable to informative dropout. Handling of reirradiated lesions in the 6 month response is not stated. Pain response is self-reported in an unblinded single-arm design.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Best read as a strategy: **4Gy first, escalate on failure**. A 63% response at 4 weeks after reirradiation suggests the low first dose did not obviously compromise salvage, at the cost of time (median 95 days to relief after reRT). It does not settle whether 4Gy matches conventional dosing up front, or whether it spares marrow.

studies.interpretation:
The premise is marrow sparing. Myeloma is a marrow disease treated with serial myelosuppressive lines, and the abstract cites data that a bone marrow dose of 10 Gy causes hematologic toxicity, so a palliative dose well under that level has a rationale that does not exist for most solid-tumor bone metastases. The concept is borrowed from indolent lymphoma, where FoRT tested ultralow-dose RT against a conventional dose, and from the general radiosensitivity of plasma cell disease. What the abstract does not deliver is the marrow endpoint itself: the only safety statement is the absence of grade 3+ treatment-related toxicity, with no blood count data, so the hypothesis that motivated the dose is asserted and not shown.

The efficacy read depends on which denominator you accept. Per protocol, response climbs from 59% at 4 weeks to 63% at 8 weeks and 82% at 6 months, and the authors conclude that the proportion with improved pain increased over time. By intention to treat, the same lesions give 40/70 (57%), 33/70 (47%) and 37/70 (53%), because 18/70 (26%) and then 25/70 (36%) did not complete the later assessments. An apparent rise built on a shrinking denominator is the usual signature of informative dropout: pts whose pain is controlled keep returning questionnaires, and those who progressed, were reirradiated, or deteriorated may not. The abstract does not say why assessments were missed, so the 82% is better treated as a ceiling and the 53% as a floor.

Two further details complicate the durability claim. The median time to pain relief was 36 days, which falls after the 4-week primary assessment, so the primary endpoint may undercount eventual responders while also telling you relief is slow for a symptomatic pt. And 24% received a second course, at a median dose of 20Gy and a median of 71 days after the 4Gy treatment. The abstract does not state whether a lesion that responded only after reirradiation counts as a responder at 6 months. If it does, part of the late response belongs to the higher-dose second course and not to 4Gy.

The fairest framing is a strategy trial: 4Gy first, escalate on failure. Read that way, the relevant facts are that the first step worked at 4 weeks in 40/70 lesions by ITT and that reirradiation produced a 63% response at 4 weeks, which suggests the low first dose did not obviously compromise salvage. The cost is time: median time to relief after reirradiation was 95 days. Without a randomised arm there is no way to know how many nonresponders would have responded up front to a conventional regimen, and that is the comparison a radiation oncologist needs before changing a default.

Population matters for transfer. This was a favorable group: 89% ECOG 0-1, a median of 1 prior line, uncomplicated lesions only, median baseline BPI 4.8. Nothing here speaks to complicated lesions, where structural or neurologic risk and not analgesia alone drives the dose. Accrual ran from 4/2019 to 9/2025 across 7 institutions to reach 63 evaluable pts, a pace that hints at selective enrollment. The result justifies a randomised comparison with marrow and pain endpoints; on its own it supports the approach as an option in selected pts, not as a replacement for standard palliative dosing.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The ITT read runs opposite to the abstract's framing: CR+PR was 40/70 (57%) at 4 wks, 33/70 (47%) at 8 wks and 37/70 (53%) at 6 mo, with 25/70 (36%) not completing the 6 mo assessment. The decision in play is 4Gy first with reRT held in reserve; 24% needed a second course.

open_questions: 4Gy vs conventional palliative fractionation in MM bone lesions: randomised comparison needed
Does 4Gy reduce hematologic toxicity vs higher-dose palliative RT?
Which lesions fail 4Gy and need reirradiation?
